intro: This guide helps you lead thirteen weekly sessions on Amy Carmichael (For Teens), the true story of a strong-willed girl from the coast of County Down who went to South India in 1895, never came home, and built the Dohnavur Fellowship, a home for hundreds of children, beginning with one seven-year-old who walked through the dark to find her. It is written for teens aged about 13 to 18, and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. The book tells her story honestly, faults and all, and gives teens plenty to think about: unanswered prayer, calling, faithfulness without results, cost, grief and how strong people lead.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10–15 minutes). Do the activity (about 10 minutes). Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand, and look over the questions and the activity so you know what you’ll need; most weeks need only paper and pens. Some chapters need extra care. Chapter 9 deals with girls dedicated to temples and drawn into sexual exploitation; it is written without lurid detail, but read it first, keep the talk on the book’s own words, and make sure your group knows who they can go to if they or someone they know is unsafe. Other chapters tell of converts cast out by their families, of young believers and children who died, of Amy’s chronic pain and of deep grief, so never press anyone to share their own family story or losses in front of the group. The book is careful to be fair to Hindu families and Indian culture, and to name the Indians who led the fight against temple dedication; help your group speak about Hinduism with the same respect, and welcome honest disagreement about Amy’s faults as well as her faith.

weeks.summary: Amy Carmichael grows up the eldest of seven in a Presbyterian family in Millisle, Ireland, a lively, strong-willed girl who expects God to answer prayer. When she prays for blue eyes and wakes to find them still brown, she learns that no is an answer too, and the chapter is careful not to give every unanswered prayer a neat explanation. At fifteen, at a children’s mission in Harrogate, she understands that God’s love is meant for her personally and receives it. The big idea: God is free, his refusals can be trusted, and the faith we grew up around has to become our own.

memory_verse.text: I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well.

activity.title: When God Says No
steps: Ask the group to call out reasons people give for why God doesn’t answer some prayers, and write them on one sheet without comment.
Go through the list together and sort each reason into “helpful,” “unhelpful” or “not sure.”
Read aloud the chapter’s line that God “is not a vending machine” and ask which reasons on the list treat him like one.
Give each person a moment to write down privately, for themselves, one prayer where the answer was no, and whether they still trust God with it.

weeks.summary: After her father’s death leaves the family in debt, seventeen-year-old Amy helps an old woman carry her bundle home from church and, hot with embarrassment, is struck by Paul’s words about gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay and stubble. She settles something with God that day and begins a Sunday class for the shawlies, mill girls who felt unwelcome among the church hats. The class grows until a hall called the Welcome is built for them. The big idea: what lasts is not what looks respectable but the love that bends down to serve the people others overlook.

memory_verse.text: Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw— each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.

activity.title: Gold or Stubble?
steps: Write two headings on a sheet: “Gold” (lasts) and “Stubble” (burns up).

Read out a list of things teens spend energy on, such as likes on a post, a good grade, helping a sibling, a reputation, a friendship with someone left out, and let the group decide where each one goes.
Talk about the ones that are hard to place, and what would make the same activity gold or stubble.
Ask everyone to write down privately one “shawlie” in their world, someone left out, and one small way to welcome them this week.

weeks.summary: Amy wears herself out living among mill workers in Manchester and is taken in by Robert Wilson, a Keswick founder who treats her as a daughter. In January 1892 the words “Go ye” come to her with force; her widowed mother gives her freely to God, while Wilson and some friends struggle with her going. The China Inland Mission turns her down on medical grounds, but the Keswick Convention sends her to Japan in 1893. The big idea: God’s call is to go and tell, not to be successful, and our going nearly always costs someone else something too.

memory_verse.text: And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation.”

activity.title: Two Good Things
steps: Explain that Amy had to choose between two good things: caring for Robert Wilson and obeying the call to go.
Split the group into two sides. One side argues for Amy staying with the Dear Old Man; the other argues for her going.
Give each side two minutes to make its best case, then swap sides and argue the other view.
Finish by asking: what made this choice hard, and who in your life has made room for you to do something hard?

weeks.summary: In Japan Amy depends on Japanese Christians to interpret, decides her English clothes are getting in the way and starts wearing Japanese dress, and battles illness and slow results. She says that in a cave in the hills God gave her a promise against loneliness. When her health breaks, she leaves for Shanghai and Ceylon without consulting the committee that sent her, then is called home when Wilson has a stroke, before finally being accepted for India in 1895. The big idea: God directs our paths even through false starts, but feeling guided doesn’t excuse us from talking to the people responsible for us.

memory_verse.text: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.

activity.title: Map the Zigzag
steps: Draw Amy’s route together as a zigzag line: Belfast, Manchester, China (closed), Japan, Ceylon, home, India.
At each turn, write one word for how it might have felt to her at the time.
Talk about where she listened to others and where she skipped that step.
Ask each person to sketch privately a zigzag from their own life, a plan that fell through, and to note one older person they could talk to before their next big decision.

weeks.summary: In India Amy is uneasy with missionaries who live apart from Indian people, though the chapter notes she was not always fair. Under Thomas Walker she learns Tamil and travels the villages by bullock cart with a band of Indian Christian women led by Ponnammal. Day after day they see few results, and she clings to the text that stewards must be faithful, rejoicing that it doesn’t say “successful.” The big idea: God doesn’t ask us to be impressive; he asks us to be faithful in ordinary, unseen work.

memory_verse.text: Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.

activity.title: Highlight Reel or Real Day?
steps: Ask everyone to write a three-line “highlight reel” version of last week, the way it might look online.
Now ask them to write three honest lines about what most of the week was really like.
Without sharing details, talk about why we prefer the first version, and why Amy refused to write that way.
Have each person choose one ordinary, faithful habit to keep every day this week and write it where they will see it.

weeks.summary: As young people begin to show interest in the gospel, their families push back: a boy is hastily married off, a girl Amy calls Treasure cannot be protected because her age cannot be proved, and a son is flogged and offered his inheritance to return. The chapter asks readers to see these families fairly, as people acting out of love and fear. Two boys are baptised and die of cholera weeks later, and Amy asks whether it was worth it, believing they would say Jesus’ welcome made it so. The big idea: Jesus promises a hundredfold, but “with persecutions,” and for many believers faith still costs family, home and safety.

memory_verse.text: Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life.”

activity.title: Praying for the Persecuted
activity.materials: A world map or phone to look up information
steps: In pairs, look up one country where becoming a Christian is dangerous today.
Have each pair share two or three facts with the group about what believers there face.
Discuss: why does the chapter ask us to read the families in Amy’s stories fairly, rather than as villains?
Pray together for believers in the countries you found, and for their families too.

weeks.summary: In March 1901 a seven-year-old girl who had been given to temple women as a baby runs away and finds Amy, saying, “I have come to stay.” She had been punished cruelly and was afraid of being “married to the god.” When the temple women come to take her back, she refuses, and Amy and the Walkers decide to keep her and face the legal risk; the only debt claimed against her turns out to be fourpence halfpenny. The big idea: God cares for the helpless, and everything Amy is remembered for began with one child.

memory_verse.text: But you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself; you have been the helper of the fatherless.

activity.title: Who Protects Children?
steps: Ask the group to list people and places that exist to keep children safe today, from teachers to helplines to charities.
In pairs, look up one organisation that protects children at risk, near you or abroad.
Have each pair tell the group what it does and one practical way young people can support it.
Close by praying for those organisations by name.

weeks.summary: The household settles at Dohnavur, and Amy gives up her village travelling to care for the children who keep arriving. Her book Things as They Are (1903) refuses to dress up the mission and names hard realities, and Eugene Stock’s preface says it is the truth but not the whole truth. The chapter also asks how the book would read to a Hindu, noting that Amy was sometimes unfair to Hinduism even as she wrote warmly of Hindu people. The big idea: tell the truth without polishing it, and tell it fairly about others too.

memory_verse.text: But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.

activity.title: Fair Description Test
steps: Ask each person to write two sentences describing their own church or youth group honestly, including one hard part.
Next, ask them to write two sentences describing another faith or group they know a little about.
Read the second sentences aloud anonymously and ask: would a person who belongs to that faith or group recognise this as fair?
Talk about how Amy could be both truthful and unfair, and how we can avoid that.

weeks.summary: This chapter tells honestly how the old tradition of temple dedication, once honoured and artistic, had changed so that many young girls were given to temples and later exploited. Amy met it through children, never published what she learned, and took girls in one at a time. The campaign that ended it was led by Indians such as Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy and Moovalur Ramamirtham, and the 1947 law should be remembered as theirs; the chapter also notes that not everyone in those communities welcomed the reform. The big idea: once we know about an evil, we are responsible, and we can oppose it without despising the people around it.

memory_verse.text: Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter.

activity.title: Who Can I Tell?
steps: Read Proverbs 24:11–12 aloud and ask what excuse the passage takes away.
As a group, list trusted adults and helplines in your area someone could go to if a young person were unsafe, and write them on a sheet everyone can copy.
Discuss the chapter’s point that telling a trusted adult about exploitation is not gossip.
Give everyone a moment to save or write down one name or number privately, for themselves or a friend.

weeks.summary: Preena, nicknamed the Elf, fills the household with life: she sings to keep Satan away, counts sins and blessings on her fingers, argues that Ruth shows love matters more than obedience, and asks why she was naughty when she prayed to be good. Babies begin to arrive, nurseries are built, and the children grow up as Indian Christians with Tamil names, calling Amy “Amma,” with high and low castes living as sisters. Amy is strict and sometimes exacting, but Dohnavur is mostly a happy place. The big idea: children are people, not cases or trophies, and strength needs to learn gentleness.

memory_verse.text: He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young.

activity.title: The Elf’s Questions
steps: Read out the Elf’s question: “How was it I was naughty when I wanted to be good? So what is the use of praying?”
In small groups, write the best answer you could give a seven-year-old in two or three simple sentences.
Share the answers and compare them with Paul’s struggle in Romans 7.
Challenge everyone to spend real time this week listening to a younger child’s questions about God.

weeks.summary: Between 1912 and 1915 Amy loses Thomas Walker, her mother, and her closest friend Ponnammal, whose healing she prayed for and did not receive, while the household lives under the threat of court cases and war. Amy chooses acceptance, taking from God’s hand what she cannot understand. For six years she prays about boys exploited through temples and drama companies, and in 1918 a baby boy is brought to Dohnavur and the boys’ work begins. The big idea: waiting and grieving without understanding is not failing at faith; it is where faith lives.

memory_verse.text: Jesus answered him, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.”

activity.title: Not Now, But Afterward
steps: Give everyone a sheet and ask them to fold it in half, labelling one side “Now” and the other “Afterward.”
On the “Now” side, have them write privately one thing they are waiting on God for or don’t understand.
On the “Afterward” side, have them copy out John 13:7.
Discuss together: what is the difference between giving up and the acceptance Amy chose? Then let people keep their sheets.

weeks.summary: Amy founds the Sisters of the Common Life, and the work becomes the independent Dohnavur Fellowship, which takes no salaries and makes no appeals. Her bitter parting with the gifted young Stephen Neill, who later became a bishop and historian, shows her difficulty sharing authority and telling disagreement from disloyalty, and some wondered whether Dohnavur’s walls stayed too high. At the same time the Fellowship builds a hospital serving Hindus and Christians alike. The big idea: leaders are called to be examples, not to lord it over others, and being sure you’re right is not the same as being right.

memory_verse.text: Not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.

activity.title: Lead or Lord It?
steps: Read out short scenarios: a group project captain, a team leader, an older sibling, a worship band leader, each facing someone who disagrees.
For each one, have the group suggest a “lording it” response and an “example” response.
Discuss which is easier and why the chapter says strong people find this especially hard.
Ask everyone to think privately of one person who recently disagreed with them and plan to ask them to explain their view again.

weeks.summary: In 1931 Amy falls into an uncovered pit and is left mostly bedridden for almost twenty years, writing books like Gold Cord, Rose from Brier and If, and growing in gentleness while learning to let go of control. She lives to see Indian independence and the Madras Act, dies at Dohnavur in 1951, and is buried under a bird-bath marked “Amma.” The chapter weighs her life honestly: hundreds of children given a home and faith, alongside real faults. The big idea: like a grain of wheat, what we let go of for Christ can bear much fruit.

memory_verse.text: Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

activity.title: One Word
steps: Recall that Amy’s grave carries a single word: Amma.
Ask each person to write down privately one word they would want written over their life.
As a group, look back over the thirteen weeks and list the things Amy let go of, and what grew from each.
Invite everyone to write, for themselves, one thing they are holding tightly that God may be asking them to loosen, and one small step toward it.
